issues.subcategory: simulated data presented as findings
issues.description: The entire results section, and the abstract's reported findings, are based on randomly generated Qualtrics data, not real participant responses. Despite repeated warnings embedded in the document, the manuscript presents specific statistics, conclusions, and figures as if they were empirical findings. This makes every reported result, effect size, confidence interval, and conclusion scientifically meaningless. Publishing or submitting a manuscript with fabricated results—even if acknowledged internally—is deeply misleading and violates basic norms of scientific reporting.
issues.quote: We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: self-selection into conditions
issues.description: The procedures section states that 'participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.' This is not random assignment—it is self-selection, which fundamentally destroys the study's ability to make causal inferences. Participants who choose to learn about the identifiable victim effect may systematically differ from those who do not (e.g., in curiosity, prior knowledge, or openness to persuasion). Similarly, those who choose to read about an identifiable victim may differ from those who choose statistical victims. The original studies used random assignment; this deviation makes the replication a quasi-experiment at best and invalidates any comparison with the original causal claims.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: within-subjects design for identifiability manipulation
issues.description: The original studies used a between-subjects design: each participant encountered only one victim type (identifiable or statistical). This replication embeds Studies 1 and 3 into a single within-subjects design. If participants encounter both identifiable and statistical victims, they explicitly compare them, fundamentally altering the psychological mechanism being studied. The identifiable victim effect is precisely about how isolated presentation of a single victim elicits disproportionate affect; within-subjects exposure triggers analytical comparison and demand characteristics, eliminating the very process the study aims to measure. This is a critical methodological deviation that cannot be treated as a 'close replication.'
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables.

issues.subcategory: simulated findings presented as real in abstract and results
issues.description: The abstract and results sections are written in the past tense and present specific numerical findings (e.g., 'Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim') as if they are real empirical outcomes. Readers encountering this document without the embedded warnings would have no indication the findings are fabricated. The manuscript should never be in a state where simulated results are written as concluded scientific findings, especially with authorial declarations that no conflicts of interest exist and data collection was completed before analysis.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: hypothetical vs. real donation
issues.description: The original studies had participants actually donate real money (up to $5 received from a prior survey) to Save the Children via a charity request letter. This replication replaces real donations with imaginary ones ('Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5'). There is extensive evidence in behavioral economics and decision-making research that hypothetical and real monetary decisions differ substantially (e.g., hypothetical bias). The affective engagement and decision weight attached to a real sacrifice of money is qualitatively different from a purely hypothetical statement. This deviation is large enough to compromise comparability with the original findings and should be classified as a major moderator of the identifiable victim effect, not a minor procedural adjustment.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: merging two distinct experimental designs into one study
issues.description: Study 1 and Study 3 of Small et al. (2007) tested fundamentally different mechanisms: Study 1 tested explicit education about the identifiable victim effect, while Study 3 tested implicit debiasing through joint presentation of victim types. These are not simply additive manipulations—they involve distinct psychological processes and were designed as independent experiments. Merging them into a single factorial design conflates explicit and implicit interventions, introduces order effects, and creates a design that was never validated in the original work. The replication cannot cleanly isolate either mechanism, and any failure to replicate is uninterpretable because the target design no longer matches either original study.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: direction of identifiable victim effect reversed
issues.description: The core finding of the identifiable victim effect is that people donate more to an identifiable victim than to statistical victims. In the reported 'results' (based on simulated data), this effect is reversed: 'participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).' While this arises from random data, the manuscript presents this reversal as a finding and discusses it as a replication outcome without adequately flagging that the direction contradicts the foundational effect being replicated. Even if real, such a reversal would require substantial theoretical explanation.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.subcategory: extension finding contradicts stated hypothesis
issues.description: Hypothesis 6 predicts that 'An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims.' However, the reported significant finding (Table 14) is between the statistical victim condition and the joint condition (statistical > joint), not between identifiable and statistical conditions. Neither comparison involving the identifiable victim versus the statistical victim condition is significant (Bonferroni p = 1.000). The text does not acknowledge that the actual pattern of results directly contradicts the stated hypothesis; instead, the abstract claims 'results have supported the hypothesis.' This is a logical and reporting error regardless of data quality.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: no manipulation check
issues.description: Neither the original study design description nor the replication protocol includes a manipulation check to verify that (a) the intervention successfully induced analytical/deliberative thinking versus affective processing, or (b) that participants perceived the identifiable victim as more identifiable and the statistical victim as more abstract/statistical. Without manipulation checks, any null result cannot be distinguished between a genuine failure to replicate the effect and a failure of the manipulation itself.
issues.quote: In Study 1, participants under manipulation were taught about the identifiable victim effect before donating to the victims.

issues.subcategory: implausible simulated sample demographics
issues.description: The simulated sample has a mean age of 67.80 years (SD=30.10) with an age range of 18–120. No living person reaches age 120 reliably (the oldest verified human was 122 years old, an extreme outlier), and an age range to 120 is nonsensical for a survey. Furthermore, a mean age of nearly 68 is wildly implausible for an MTurk sample, which typically averages 30–35 years. This demonstrates the random nature of the data and highlights that these 'participant' characteristics were never reviewed for plausibility before being reported. The SD of 30.10 is also unrealistically large.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males).

issues.subcategory: confidence interval spans zero but result declared significant
issues.description: In Table 14, the post-hoc comparison 'Statistical VS Joint' yields a Cohen's d = 0.08 with a 95% CI of [-0.07, 0.23]. This confidence interval spans zero, indicating the effect size is not significantly different from zero at the 95% confidence level for d. Yet the Bonferroni-adjusted p-value is reported as .041* and the result is described as significant. This apparent contradiction likely arises from the CI being computed for d using a different formula or degrees of freedom than the t-test p-value, but it is not explained and creates confusion about the actual conclusion. CIs for effect sizes and significance tests should be consistent.

issues.subcategory: multiple comparisons without family-wise correction across ANOVAs
issues.description: Table 13 reports six separate 2x3 ANOVAs (one for each feeling variable: upsetting, sympathy, touched, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, perceived impact) across three effects (identifiability, intervention, interaction), yielding 18 F-tests. No family-wise error correction (e.g., Bonferroni, FDR) is applied across these multiple ANOVAs. With 18 tests at α = .05, the probability of at least one false positive is approximately 60%. The one significant result (perceived impact of identifiability, p = .045) is barely below .05 and is precisely the type of finding most vulnerable to Type I error in this context.
issues.quote: Perceived impact (Extension) | 2 | 3.11 | .006 | [0.00,0.02] | .045*

issues.subcategory: ordered probit regression omitted without adequate justification
issues.description: The original study used ordered probit regression as a primary analysis to account for the ordinal, discrete nature of the donation variable (0–5 integer values). The replication states 'This test would not be conducted in the replication' without providing a substantive methodological justification. Using standard ANOVA/t-tests on an ordinal outcome (donations from $0–$5) violates assumptions of continuous outcome variables. The original authors specifically chose probit regression because of the distributional properties of donations; ignoring this choice reduces analytical comparability and may produce misleading F-statistics.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression | a. effect of identifiability on donation | This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: online MTurk vs. laboratory with real stakes
issues.description: The original study was conducted in a student center laboratory where participants received actual money ($5 from a prior survey) and donated by placing bills in an envelope. This replication uses Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) for an online survey with imaginary donations. This combines two major deviations: (1) the online/laboratory context, which affects social presence, anonymity, and attentiveness; and (2) MTurk workers, who are a distinctive population known to respond to demand characteristics and show high rates of inattention. These deviations together may substantially moderate effect sizes and are not minor procedural details.
issues.quote: Online survey: Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania.

issues.subcategory: intervention applied to joint condition without original precedent
issues.description: The authors add the explicit intervention (education about the identifiable victim effect) to the joint condition, which did not exist in the original Study 3. This creates a new cell (joint/intervention) that was never tested in the original work and introduces a novel crossing of manipulations not grounded in any theoretical prediction from the original paper. This untested combination confounds the replication and may generate results that cannot be compared to any baseline from the original study.
issues.quote: Intervention applied to the joint condition: To combine study 1 and 3 into a single study, intervention will be applied to the joint condition to allow the comparison of explicit and implicit manipulation with fewer confounds.

issues.subcategory: updated victim stimuli
issues.description: The replication uses updated victim information from the Save the Children website rather than the specific stimulus materials used in the original study. The identifiable victim effect is known to be highly sensitive to the specific details of victim presentation (name, age, face, story). Using different victim descriptions changes the specific emotional stimuli in an uncontrolled way. While described as a 'similar' deviation, this could systematically alter the magnitude of affect generated and thus the size of the effect. The original stimuli should be used or their unavailability explicitly justified.
issues.quote: Updated victim information: We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children given that those used in the original study was dated two decades ago.

issues.subcategory: availability heuristic incorrectly applied to explain identifiable victim effect
issues.description: The introduction invokes the availability heuristic (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) to explain why an identifiable victim generates stronger affective responses than statistical victims. The availability heuristic is about ease of retrieving instances from memory to estimate frequency or probability—it is not the primary mechanism for the identifiable victim effect. The standard explanation involves the affect heuristic (Slovic et al., 2007), the singularity effect, or proportion dominance, all of which are explicitly discussed in Small et al. (2007). Misattributing the mechanism undermines the theoretical framing and misrepresents the literature.
issues.quote: The 'availability heuristic' (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual.

issues.subcategory: effect sizes dramatically smaller than original with no discussion
issues.description: The original study reported ηp2 = .06 for the effect of identifiability on donation. The replication reports ηp2 = .007—approximately an eight-fold reduction. Similarly, the original intervention effect was ηp2 = .04; the replication finds ηp2 = .001. While these are random data and thus uninterpretable, the pattern of uniformly tiny effect sizes across all outcomes (most ηp2 ≤ .008) is not discussed in terms of what this would mean for replication evaluation or power. An actual replication showing effects of this magnitude would strongly disconfirm the original study.
issues.quote: Identifiability Original study | 1 | 6.75 | <.05* | .06 | N/A / Replication | 2 | 3.58 | .028* | .007 | [0.00, 0.02]

issues.subcategory: Table 1 misformats ANOVA statistics at the group level
issues.description: In Table 1, the F-statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and ηp2 from the identifiability main effect ANOVA (F(1,115)=6.75, p<.05, ηp2=.06) are repeated identically for both the 'Identifiable victim' and 'Statistical victim' rows, alongside their group means and SDs. These test statistics represent a single omnibus test, not separate tests for each group. Presenting them this way implies each group's mean was independently tested, which is incorrect and misleading. The means/SDs and the ANOVA statistics should be in separate sections of the table.

issues.subcategory: correlation analyses conducted without multiple comparison correction
issues.description: Table 15 reports Pearson correlations between aggregated feelings and donation across six conditions, yielding six separate significance tests. No correction for multiple comparisons (e.g., Bonferroni, FDR) is applied. At α = .05 with six tests, the expected number of false positives is 0.3, but the per-family error rate is approximately 26%. This is particularly problematic since the original study reported a significant correlation in only one of four conditions (r = .55, identifiable/no intervention), and the replication uses these tests to evaluate whether affective feelings predict donation.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.subcategory: power analysis not included in main text
issues.description: The manuscript states that power analysis is available only in supplementary materials, but provides no summary of minimum required sample size, assumed effect size, or achieved power in the main text. Power analysis is essential for evaluating whether the study was designed to detect the effects of interest. Without it in the main text, readers cannot assess whether observed null results reflect genuine absence of effects or inadequate power. This is especially important for a replication study where power to detect the original effect size is the key methodological question.
issues.quote: To obtain the minimal sample size required for this study, The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary.

issues.subcategory: repeated misspelling of author name 'Slovic' as 'Solvic'
issues.description: The name 'Slovic' is misspelled as 'Solvic' multiple times throughout the manuscript, including in substantive citations ('Solvic (2007)', 'Solvic, 2010'). This creates citation errors—'Solvic (2010)' appears to be cited in the literature review but is not listed in the reference section. This compromises bibliographic accuracy and suggests insufficient proofreading.
issues.quote: Solvic (2007) argued for the drawbacks of the phenomenon... Solvic (2007) urged the public not to rely on our unreliable emotional responses.

issues.subcategory: no pre-survey compensation for donation pool
issues.description: In the original studies, participants received $5 from a prior unrelated survey, which they could then donate. This design feature was theoretically important: the money was 'found money' given before donation decisions, creating a realistic sense of having real resources to donate. In this replication, no compensation is provided and no realistic donation pool exists. This changes the psychological context of the decision from 'how much of this money I actually have do I give?' to a purely imaginary exercise, reducing ecological validity and the affective reality of the sacrifice.
issues.quote: No reward acquired from a pre-survey: Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation.

issues.subcategory: hypothesis 5a contains logical error
issues.description: Hypothesis 5a states 'An identifiable victim elicits more affective feelings than an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics and statistical victims.' This compares the identifiable victim to both (a) an identifiable victim with statistics and (b) statistical victims, which is a reasonable comparison set. However, this is listed as Hypothesis 5a while 5b concerns the effect of the intervention on feelings. The hypotheses are not clearly delineated in terms of which statistical test each maps onto (e.g., which ANOVA contrast corresponds to 5a vs. 5b), making pre-registered hypothesis evaluation ambiguous.
issues.quote: 5a: An identifiable victim elicits more affective feelings than an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics and statistical victims

issues.subcategory: descriptive statistics in post-hoc text do not match Table 7
issues.description: In the results text, the identifiable victim condition is described as having M=2.24, SD=1.67 and the statistical victim condition as M=2.54, SD=1.76. However, Table 7 shows different means: for the identifiable victim condition, intervention=2.58 and no intervention=2.50 (average ≈ 2.54), and for the statistical victim condition, intervention=2.46 and no intervention=2.01 (average ≈ 2.24). The means appear to be swapped or incorrectly aggregated in the text relative to Table 7, creating internal inconsistency in the reported results.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.subcategory: incomplete manuscript with placeholder links
issues.description: Several critical links are left as placeholders ('enter link here') for the cloud folder for the presentation and peer reviews. These sections are incomplete at the time of manuscript submission. Additionally, the supplementary document is linked but its content cannot be independently verified. An incomplete manuscript with broken or missing links for materials, code, and reviews does not meet transparency and open science standards.
issues.quote: Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here> / Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here>

issues.subcategory: ηp2 reported with insufficient decimal precision for small effects
issues.description: Several effect sizes are reported as ηp2 = 0 or ηp2 = .001 or .002, yet confidence intervals are reported as [0.00, 0.01] or [0.00, 0.00]. Reporting effect sizes rounded to three decimal places when they are near zero is insufficient—it does not allow readers to distinguish between, for example, ηp2 = .0001 and ηp2 = .0009. At minimum, additional significant figures or an explicit statement that effects were negligible would aid interpretation.

issues.subcategory: student identification number included in manuscript
issues.description: The manuscript includes a student ID number (3035682015) in the author information table, which is a potential privacy concern. Student ID numbers are typically considered personally identifiable institutional information and should not be published in academic manuscripts.
issues.quote: Yik Chun | Wong | ... | 3035682015

issues.subcategory: typos and grammatical errors affecting clarity
issues.description: The manuscript contains multiple grammatical errors and typos that impair readability and professional quality: 'asserts are accumulated' should be 'assets are accumulated'; 'Hypothese 3 and 4' should be 'Hypotheses 3 and 4'; 'fill up a questionnaire' is non-standard; 'The study described in the current report is close to very close replication' is grammatically incomplete; 'the area of moral psychology' misclassifies judgment and decision making research. These errors suggest insufficient proofreading.
issues.quote: the lack of efficiency in resource allocation when asserts are accumulated on a single victim

issues.subcategory: missing citation in reference list
issues.description: 'Solvic (2010)' is cited in the introduction ('Solvic, 2010') within a parenthetical citation but does not appear in the reference list. Whether this is a misspelling of Slovic (2010) or a different work entirely is unclear, but no Slovic 2010 article is listed in the references either. This is a citation error that prevents readers from locating the source.
issues.quote: numerous empirical research (Friedrich & McGuire, 2010; Lee & Feeley, 2016; Solvic, 2010)

issues.subcategory: Table 4 has duplicate columns for same data
issues.description: Table 4 is intended to compare the original study to the replication, but it contains two identical columns both labeled 'Qualtrics generated response' with identical values (e.g., sample size listed twice as '1000 | 1000'). This appears to be a formatting/template error that was not corrected, making the table confusing and redundant.
issues.quote: Sample size | Study 1: 121 Study 3: 159 | 1000 | 1000

issues.subcategory: pre-registration status inconsistency
issues.description: The authorship declaration states 'Gilad supervised each step in the project, conducted the pre-registrations, and ran data collection,' implying data collection occurred. Yet the Methods and Results sections contain the warning that all content is based on simulated data 'to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection.' It is unclear whether data collection actually occurred, and the manuscript cannot be evaluated as a completed study. The word count listed as 'manuscript - [7394]' uses brackets suggesting it was never finalized.
issues.quote: Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period... [IMPORTANT: Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection.]
